segs.text: This is the most productive person on the internet. Three hundred million subscribers. Videos that cost more than films. A pace nobody in the industry has matched.
I'm probably one of the least energetic people you'll ever meet.
segs.speaker: subject

segs.text: He is not being modest. Since he was fifteen, his own immune system has been attacking him from the inside, and there are days it wins.
So this is not a story about a workout. It is a story about a body that kept taking things away from a kid, and what he did to take some of it back.
Before any of it, he was an athlete. A kid who played constantly, and who assumed — the way you do at that age — that his body would keep doing whatever he asked of it.
I played baseball nonstop, and then when I got Crohn's I lost like 50 pounds.
segs.speaker: subject

segs.text: The diagnosis had a name. Crohn's disease. What it was doing to him is the part almost nobody explains — and we will, properly, in a minute. First, what it took.

When I turned 15, I got Crohn's and I went from like 190 pounds down to 139. I lost all muscle I had, and so I was like, all right, I'm not playing baseball in college anymore. So then I was like, it's just all in on YouTube.
segs.speaker: subject

segs.text: That is the whole pivot, in about ten seconds. A body. A future closing. A decision. He did not choose the internet over baseball. Baseball was taken, and the internet was what was left.
Most videos skip this part, because it is not inspiring. But you cannot understand anything he did later without sitting in it first.

When I was 15, I just started going to the bathroom eight, nine, ten times a day, not digesting any food because my GI tract is literally just attacking itself. Your immune system in your gut thinks your gut is a foreign invader, and so it just starts attacking itself.
segs.speaker: subject

segs.text: Not discomfort. A body that will not keep what you feed it. You can eat and still starve. And while everyone around him grew into their frames, his was being subtracted.

Here is what is actually happening inside him. Crohn's is an inflammatory bowel disease. The immune system — the part of you built to attack infections — misidentifies the lining of your own digestive tract as the enemy and attacks that instead.

And it does not attack the surface only. The inflammation goes through the entire thickness of the bowel wall. That wall thickens, narrows, and scars, so the passage through it gets tighter — and the tissue that is supposed to pull nutrients out of your food stops being able to do it.

Which is the part that explains a teenager losing fifty pounds. He was eating. The food was going through him without ever being absorbed. His body was starving with a full stomach — and taking his muscle apart to stay alive.

It also does not run on a schedule. It flares and it quiets, and the Crohn's and Colitis Foundation is clear that severity varies enormously between patients. You cannot plan around it. It arrives when it arrives.
Sometimes I'll flare up and then I'm just like, I'm dead. I just lay in bed all day, and I can't really do anything.
segs.speaker: subject

segs.text: Hundreds of thousands of Americans live with this. There is no cure. Not a difficult cure, not an expensive one — there isn't one. There is only management, and management has a cost of its own.
I'm on what's called Remicade, and so every eight weeks they just do an IV with a huge bag, which essentially suppresses my immune system.
segs.speaker: subject

segs.text: For the rest of his life. The only way to call off a defence system that has turned on you is to shut the whole thing down — which means everything else gets in more easily. He has traded one illness for a permanent open door.
Corn. Anything spicy. Anything like overly, overly processed.
segs.speaker: subject

segs.text: This is the part people underestimate. Not the pain. The permanence. Every meal, every year, forever, checked against a list.
Now put everything you just heard underneath what he did next. Because he did not do it after he got better. There was no after.
I was as awkward as they came—no money, no nothing—and I just basically obsessed over YouTube every day for a decade.
segs.speaker: subject

segs.text: Ten years of treating one problem as solvable — testing, failing, rebuilding — carried out by someone who has already told you he runs out of energy walking across a room.

I didn't talk to anyone. I hardly had any friends because I was so obsessed with YouTube. Back then, no one cared. I thought I didn't even know how to speak. I couldn't hold a conversation because people would tell me, all you talk about is YouTube.
segs.speaker: subject

segs.text: The machine he built was extraordinary, and it was hungry, and the first thing it ate was everything that was not the machine. Including him.
A man who could optimise anything, running a system that consumed every hour, inside a body he had never been able to optimise at all. Something was going to break.
I was so laser-focused on the channel, and I just realized one day: I have not been working out or taking care of myself. Then I called Eric and I was like, this is a problem. Let's do this.
segs.speaker: subject

segs.text: Notice what the fix was not. Not motivation. Not a new year. It was a second person and a rule — because he already knew his own intentions were not reliable enough to bet on.
I signed a legally binding contract with MrBeast that says that we both have to work out every single day for 600 days.
segs.speaker: support

segs.text: Signed, with a penalty attached.
That contract says that if I miss a single day of working out, I have to get MrBeast's name tattooed on my forehead.
segs.speaker: support

segs.text: Another man's name, on your face, permanently. It sounds like a bit. It is good behavioural engineering — make quitting immediate, public and irreversible, and the worst day stops being a decision.

Today was day 310. Me and Eric signed a contract: we'd work out every day, and if we didn't we'd get a tattoo of each other. You're okay to have a day off if it's an actual part of your program, so occasionally we have rest days. For the most part, we've worked out every single day and held each other accountable.
segs.speaker: subject

segs.text: One correction the internet always drops. That was not three hundred and ten unbroken sessions. Programmed rest counted, deliberately, from the start. A plan that treats recovery as failure is not a plan. It is a countdown to injury.
So what does he actually do? Most videos invent this part. Here is only what he has said himself.

Right now it's really three things that my entire world revolves around: I work out every day, I work on main-channel videos, and I work on Feastables. I wake up, I do that, and when I'm done I go to bed.
segs.speaker: subject

segs.text: In a life that had previously had room for exactly one.

In the short term, I'd probably upload more and get more done if I didn't work out. It's like an hour and a half every day, and then the food, and I do 15,000 steps a day. All that is very time-consuming.
segs.speaker: subject

segs.text: The number that should stop you is not the step count. It is the admission attached to it. He knew this was costing him uploads and did it anyway. For a person whose entire identity was output, choosing to produce less is the most radical thing in this story.
Up to this point, I've just been losing fat. It's a lot harder to put on muscle when you're losing fat.
segs.speaker: subject

segs.text: And the limits of the record, stated plainly: he has never published a training split, a set and rep scheme, or a calorie target. Any video handing you one is filling in blanks. What he has described is a system — train, rest, walk, eat within the rules his body set.
MrBeastProtocolCard

All you have to do, really, is work out for like three months really consistently, and then it'll just become part of your lifestyle. A year ago I couldn't fathom how I was ever going to do this religiously. But now it's truly a habit.
segs.speaker: subject

segs.text: A season. That is all it takes to stop deciding, and it is the mechanism underneath everything else here. Not discipline as a personality trait. Repetition, continued until the choice disappears.
And then the story does something a transformation video would never allow. It stops working.

Way harder—infinitely harder. I thought I'd just work out for like an hour and it'd be relatively easy, but it's very time-consuming because we're trying to get what normal people would get, gains-wise, in like two years in one.
segs.speaker: subject

segs.text: He had modelled it the way he models everything. Input, time, output. Bodies do not read the spreadsheet — and his had a head start on refusing.

A hundred percent. I tell Alex all the time, I can't believe how little progress I've made in the amount of time. When we started, we both thought if we just went to the gym and worked out really hard, we would end up in the same spot. We were so stupid.
segs.speaker: subject

segs.text: Sit with how strange that is. The man whose entire brand is that enough effort beats any problem, saying on camera that he put in the effort and the problem did not move. That is not modesty. That is the method failing.
And then the machine took it back.

Beast Games is such a monster of a project, and I have to maintain the same YouTube upload schedule, and then I do a lot on Feastables now and then I have a couple other businesses. So I just honestly, something had to give, and sadly it was working out.
segs.speaker: subject

segs.text: Months, it's just, it's really killing me, to be honest.
segs.speaker: subject

segs.text: Six hundred days of proof that he could do it, and it still lost to a production schedule. If you have ever built a habit you were proud of and watched it evaporate the month work got hard — that is this story, with fewer zeros.

It only needs to be 45 minutes, 5 days a week. It doesn't need to be hard, but the bigger problem is I'm just not sleeping like I used to. When I hit it hard in the gym and then I don't get enough sleep, that causes pretty extreme fatigue the next day. So it's like, I got to fix sleep first.
segs.speaker: subject

segs.text: That is not surrender. It is the first moment in the whole story where he sizes a plan to the life he actually has instead of the one he wishes he had. And notice what he refuses to fix first. It is not the training.
So — did the disease build MrBeast?

No. It took a future from a teenager and handed him nothing back. What it did was narrow the road until one path was left, and he ran down that one harder than anybody alive. That is not a gift. He has never once called it one.
You look like a different human being. I do think that we both have severely changed our life for the better, and I'm very grateful for us doing this challenge.
segs.speaker: subject

segs.text: What he got to keep is not a physique. It is a pattern. Reserve the time before the day takes it. Put the promise somewhere another person can see it. Let recovery count. Then lose it, and start again.
Oh, of course. I mean, mostly because I just don't want to die.
segs.speaker: subject

segs.text: Not to look good. Not for a thumbnail. Because his body has spent a decade trying to shut him down, and training is one of the few arguments he still gets to win.
Honestly, I haven't really thought about it. It's just one of those things - I'm so used to it. It's just life.
segs.speaker: subject

segs.text: It's just life. Said by a man who lost fifty pounds at fifteen, built the biggest channel on earth exhausted, and still shows up to a gym on the days his body would rather he didn't. The disease did not build him. He built himself, in spite of it — over and over, because it never stops asking him to.
If this changed how you see him, tell me in the comments which part you did not know. And subscribe — the next one is about a man whose body was the entire job, right up until it nearly ended him.
